source: Founder's own TikTok account audit (Metricool + screenshots)
what_happened: Ben audited his first TikTok posts for AfriShield. Every product-first post (founder intro, 'Meet Elodie', AI Concierge Test explainer) stalled at roughly 100–150 views. The one story-led post — the White House Douala restaurant video — drew the most comments of the batch.
problem: Posts opened with the product or the founder's title, some were under 8 seconds, one had typos in the first on-screen text, and hashtags were jammed inside caption sentences.
discovery: Nobody scrolls to meet a product. The story post outperformed on comments; the product posts never earned TikTok's second distribution wave.
result: A locked story-first script format (the afrishield-tiktok-video-script skill) and a rule to open on tension, not on the product. Retention data itself is unavailable (Metricool lacks TikTok Business analytics scope).
lesson: Lead with the customer's tension; the product is the answer at the end of the story.

source: Published TikTok about White House Restaurant, Douala (a public business, portrayed positively)
what_happened: Ben made a video using White House, a Douala restaurant brand founded in 1993 with several locations, as an example of a strong brand that owns a website rather than relying only on rented social platforms, ending with the question of whether AI would recommend it.
people_involved: White House Restaurant, Douala (public business, not a client)
problem: Most businesses build their whole presence on rented platforms they don't control.
discovery: A real, well-known local example made the abstract 'rented land vs owned property' idea land — it became the best-commented post.
lesson: A website is owned digital property, but owning it is not the same as being understood and recommended by AI.
unverified_claims: Exact list of White House locations should be re-checked against their website before reuse
possible_topics: what AI says about Douala restaurants

source: AfriShield original-data pilot study published on afrishieldai.com (DataForSEO SERP API)
what_happened: AfriShield ran 9 'best {service} in {city}' searches across Nairobi, Lagos, Accra, Johannesburg and Arusha and measured who owns page one — the business's own website or an aggregator — plus whether Google showed an AI answer.
people_involved: AfriShield (own research); businesses appear only in aggregate
problem: Nobody had published how often African businesses own their own search results versus directories and aggregators.
discovery: Travel/hospitality businesses owned about 23% of page-one results with their own sites versus 68% for professional services; Google showed an AI answer on 9 of 9 queries.
result: A published pilot study and dataset — AfriShield's first original statistics.
lesson: In tourism, aggregators own most of the search results; that is the gap AI visibility work targets. It is a 9-search pilot, so present it as a pilot.
possible_topics: who owns page one in African tourism

what_happened: AfriShield tested whether AI search would name AfriShield itself as an AI SEO / GEO agency in West, Central, East and North Africa. Across 8 buyer-intent prompts plus a brand search, AfriShield surfaced 0 times.
people_involved: AfriShield (own test); competitor agencies named only in private research
problem: An AI visibility company that AI doesn't know about.
discovery: South African agencies dominate the continental answer; a Kenyan agency already claims 'first in Africa'; nobody owns the answer in Central Africa / Cameroon; a Lagos agency's similar name creates entity confusion.
result: A starting line of zero, a Central-Africa beachhead strategy, and two on-site GEO pages published the same day. No citation result has been measured yet.
lesson: Measure before you market — and a baseline of zero is a story, not a secret.
unverified_claims: Measurement used a live web-search proxy because the geo-optimizer and DataForSEO tools failed to connect; re-run per engine before quoting per-engine numbers
possible_topics: Central Africa has no GEO incumbent

source: AfriShield lead research on West African SMBs selling through TikTok
what_happened: Ben sourced 45 real estate, fintech and e-commerce businesses selling through TikTok in Cameroon, Nigeria, Côte d'Ivoire, Senegal and Guinea. 44 of the 45 had no website; many ran high-value sales through captions and hand-typed WhatsApp, often listing two or three phone numbers in one caption.
people_involved: 45 businesses (must stay anonymous — sector and country only)
problem: Serious businesses with no owned web presence that AI or search could read.
discovery: The storefront is a caption plus a WhatsApp number; multiple unrouted phone numbers is common.
result: A lead tracker and playbook; fintech yielded few SMBs.
lesson: For West African SMBs, 'get a website' is step zero of AI visibility, and unrouted phone numbers are a missed-call problem.
possible_topics: why AI can't recommend a caption

what_happened: While building a prospect dossier, the paid-data tool's free plan blocked people search, so AfriShield scraped company websites instead. One scraped 'team list' turned out to be fabricated, and was caught and discarded during verification.
people_involved: AfriShield; the affected company must not be named
problem: AI-assisted research can return confident, invented names.
discovery: Every scraped person had to be checked against the public record; generic inboxes were the reliable output.
result: 23 verified company emails, 34 verified target companies; one fabricated list removed.
lesson: Verify every name AI or a scraper gives you before you email a stranger.

prospecting in Africa without paid data

source: Content Autopilot first gap analysis of AfriShield's own 180-day calendar
what_happened: Building the Content Autopilot, Ben ran its first audit on his own 180-day content calendar. It found calendar rows narrating events with no evidence behind them, 29 past-due days with nothing published against them while 6 posts went out off-plan, and Cameroon in only 4 of 195 items despite being the home market.
problem: A plan written in one sitting drifts from reality and invents convenient stories.
discovery: The calendar needed receipts, not more ideas.
result: Flags on every unevidenced row and a rule: link a real story, perform it on camera, or label it hypothetical.
lesson: Audit the plan against reality before adding to it.
possible_topics: I audited my own content calendar

what_happened: Ben verified a 500-lead cold-email list locally before paying for a verification service. 209 of 500 addresses were settled for free; a large share stayed unknown because the office internet connection's IP is on a spam blocklist that Microsoft 365 and Mimecast servers check.
problem: Paying to verify every address, and mistaking 'unknown' for 'invalid'.
discovery: Unknown results on corporate mail servers were caused by the sender's IP reputation, not bad addresses.
result: About 42% of the list verified with zero credits; paid credits spent only on the unknowns.
lesson: Know why a tool says 'unknown' before you throw away a third of your leads.
possible_topics: verify leads before paying for tools
